articles.title: In 2000, Taiwan used ground-up discarded tyres to make experimental asphalt roads, and a four-year study found they performed better than conventional pavements
articles.summary: Taiwan built two experimental roads using recycled tyre rubber in asphalt in 2000 and 2001, testing whether discarded tyres could be turned into a
articles.body: Taiwan built two experimental roads using recycled tyre rubber in asphalt in 2000 and 2001, testing whether discarded tyres could be turned into a material for better-performing pavements. Supported by the Taiwan Highway Bureau, the projects used ground tyre rubber in two different asphalt mixtures, with researchers monitoring their performance over four years. According to the study published in ScienceDirect, titled ‘Use of ground tire rubber in asphalt pavements: Field trial and evaluation in Taiwan’, the asphalt rubber mixtures performed better than conventional dense-graded asphalt mixes. The research also found that the recycled rubber mixtures could be successfully produced using locally sourced materials and existing paving techniques in Taiwan.How Taiwan tested recycled tyre rubber in experimental asphalt roadsWith support from the Taiwan Highway Bureau, two asphalt rubber (AR) pavement test sections were constructed as pilot projects. The first section, featuring a gap-graded design, was built in December 2000, while the second, using an open-graded design, was constructed in May 2001. Both projects were designed to examine the technical feasibility of incorporating ground tyre rubber obtained from local sources into asphalt pavement under Taiwanese conditions.The research used two different asphalt mixture designs for the demonstration projects. One employed a gap-graded mixture, while the other used an open-graded mixture. The researchers adopted Arizona Department of Transportation gradations and mix design specifications for the asphalt rubber mixtures. These were compared with a conventional dense-graded asphalt mixture designed according to Type IVb specifications of the Taiwan Highway Bureau, which had a nominal maximum aggregate size of 12.5 millimetres. The projects were intended to establish whether the recycled rubber mixtures could be successfully produced and laid using local materials and paving techniques.Four-year study tested recycled tyre rubber asphalt using the wet processFollowing construction, the research team carried out a four-year field evaluation to monitor the performance of the asphalt rubber pavement sections. The programme included field observations and measurements to assess how the mixtures performed under Taiwanese conditions. The researchers compared the demonstration pavements with conventional asphalt pavements to evaluate the technical suitability of incorporating ground tyre rubber into road construction.The study also examined the wet process, in which ground tyre rubber is blended with asphalt cement before the mixture is used for paving. The researchers implemented this method using #30-mesh ground tyre rubber, measuring approximately 0.6 millimetres. According to the paper's conclusions, the wet process was successfully implemented and considered adequate for use in Taiwan. Laboratory testing further indicated that plant-mixed asphalt rubber met most ASTM specifications. The findings provided evidence that locally sourced ground tyre rubber and asphalt could be combined to produce mixtures suitable for pavement construction.Taiwan's recycled rubber roads showed better performanceThe four-year evaluation found that the asphalt rubber test sections delivered satisfactory performance. The study's abstract states that the field results demonstrated the potential of the mixtures to replace modified asphalt in domestic applications. It also reported that the test sections performed well based on the field monitoring data collected during the evaluation period.In its conclusion, the research paper stated that ground tyre rubber-modified asphalt concrete mixtures could be successfully constructed using Arizona Department of Transportation mix gradations and design properties, alongside local materials and paving techniques. The researchers reported that these mixtures performed better than conventional dense-graded asphalt mixes. The findings therefore established the technical feasibility of using locally processed waste tyre rubber in asphalt pavement construction in Taiwan. The paper, published in 2008, presented the results as evidence that recycled tyre rubber could serve as a material in road construction while offering an alternative application for the country's discarded tyres.You use AI every day. articles.title: Footballer Raheem Sterling given suspended sentence for dangerous driving
articles.summary: Raheem Sterling was sentenced to 12 months imprisonment, suspended for 18 months, on Wednesday.
articles.body:
Former England footballer Raheem Sterling has been given a suspended sentence after admitting dangerously driving his Lamborghini while inhaling nitrous oxide from a balloon on a motorway.

The 31-year-old, from Berkshire, who later crashed into a metal gate during rush hour, gave no reaction as he was handed a 12-month jail term, suspended for 18 months, at Basingstoke Magistrates' Court.

Sterling had pleaded guilty to dangerous driving of a Lamborghini Urus and possessing nitrous oxide on the M25, the M3, the A327 and Minley Road on 28 May.

The judge said Sterling's use of the Class C drug had became a " maladaptive coping mechanism during a difficult period " in his career.

Sterling, who left the court without making any comment, was ordered to complete 100 hours unpaid work and was banned from driving for 24 months.

He was arrested after crashing near the M3 in Hampshire.

Raheem Sterling - from national icon to suspended jail sentence

District judge Kirsty Allman told the court on Wednesday that Sterling was seen at 01:10 BST at a McDonald's in Hayes driving "erratically and at speed" while inhaling from a pink balloon.

She went on: "At 7.45am, having not slept, you made a deliberate and entirely selfish decision, to drive your vehicle without adequate sleep and whilst consuming a Class C drug, nitrous oxide."

She said this exposed a "large number of road users to a significant risk of serious harm by the manner of your driving on two motorways and in peak travel time that morning".

During the September hearing, prosecutor Simon Jones said a number of calls were made between 07:45 and 08:52 BST about a black sports car and the manner it was being driven.

Witness Christopher Jennings called 999 after driving alongside Sterling's car on the M25, and "he was shocked by what he saw", Jones said, and made clear "he sighted the defendant inhaling from the balloon".

Fiona Jennings – driving on the southbound M3 – described the driving as "absolutely horrendous" and "swerving in and out of lanes", the court heard.

The court heard Sterling strayed into the central reservation of the M3, exited at junction 4A, and veered off the A327, crashing into a metal gate near a layby.

His vehicle sustained "substantial damage to the tyres and bodywork and was no longer capable of being driven", the court heard.

Sterling was taken to Basingstoke police investigation centre by officers, where he disclosed he had a "problem with nitrous oxide", said Jones.

The substance is legally sold for catering, medical and industrial purposes but is frequently used as a recreational drug, commonly known as laughing gas.

Sterling complied with an impairment test, but for a blood sample, Sterling asked to obtain legal advice before making a decision.

In the police sergeant's view "he was deliberately failing to provide a clear answer".

Sterling was later interviewed by police with legal representation present where he accepted he had been the driver and provided no comment answers about the driving.

Defending Sterling on Wednesday, Jason Bartfeld KC said there was no dispute that this was a "top category case" because of prolonged driving and "at times" serious impairment which would have been short periods within the driving.

But the defence did not accept the damage to the car was serious and said there was "confusion" over the failure to provide a specimen.

District Judge Kirsty Allman said: "I accept that your character has been positively exemplary.

"You enjoyed a highly successful professional football career and were widely regarded as a role model for many young people through your achievements and public profile."

He was given credit for his guilty pleas.

Sterling most recently played for Feyenoord in the Dutch Eredivisie, having left Chelsea in January, but made just eight appearances in the Netherlands.

In four years at Chelsea - including a season-long loan at Arsenal - he made 59 league appearances after signing from Manchester City in 2022.

With City he won four Premier League titles, having started his senior career with Liverpool before moving to Manchester in 2015.

In the 2021 Queen's Birthday Honours, Sterling was made an MBE for services to racial equality in sport.

articles.title: Former HSE chief Anne O'Connor 'instructs solicitors' after dismissal
articles.summary: A statement from former HSE chief executive Anne O'Connor was read out at an Irish parliamentary committee on Wednesday.
articles.body:
The former head of the Irish health service has said that she has instructed solicitors to bring a court application on her behalf to challenge her "unlawful termination" and to protect her "good name and reputation".

Taoiseach (Irish prime minister) Micheál Martin said on Tuesday that the Health Service Executive (HSE) board's decision to remove Anne O'Connor from her position was "unanimous".

O'Connor was appointed as chief executive in December 2025 and started the role in March of this year.

She said an HSE statement issued on Tuesday "wrongly gives the impression that I was aware that I was in an employment process".

On Tuesday, Martin told the Dáil (Irish lower house of parliament) that O'Connor's dismissal was not the "result of any singular event or issue".

He said the board's decision was based on its "assessment of performance and leadership" since O'Connor took on the role, and was "not the result of any single event or issue".

On Wednesday afternoon, Martin said "the HSE Board needs to give a very comprehensive account" of what happened, adding that he had "confidence" in the Irish Health Minister Jennifer Carroll MacNeill.

In a statement, the HSE statement said on 19 November its board "resolved to terminate" O'Connor's employment after it "formed the opinion" that her removal "was necessary for the effective and efficient performance" of the health service's statutory functions.

It said O'Connor commenced employment on 23 March 2026 under a five-year, fixed-term contract that included a 12-month probationary period - and her performance was reviewed in June and October.

In a statement issued on Wednesday, O'Connor said the "HSE disciplinary or probation policy were never mentioned to me during my employment".

"I had two routine objectives meetings in June and October 2026," she added.

"Until yesterday, I was not aware that in September the board had entered an 'escalated process' to evaluate my performance or that the minister, taoiseach and tánaiste (Irish deputy prime minister) had been told about this.

"Until a [Microsoft] Teams call with the Chair of the Board of the HSE at 7.30 am on Saturday morning, I did not know I was at risk of losing of my job.

"During that call I was told that I could resign or that my employment would be terminated at 11am."

Health minister appears before committee

Irish Minister for Health Jennifer Carroll MacNeill, appeared before an Irish parliamentary health committee on Wednesday and said she respects O'Connor's decision to take legal action.

O'Connor's statement was released as the committee was in session, Irish broadcaster RTÉ reports, and described by committee chair Pádraig Rice as "extraordinary" and "explosive".

"I respect what she is saying, and I respect obviously her right to initiate proceedings if that's what she is going to do," MacNeill said.

"That's a process obviously I fully respect. What she is describing there is her interaction with the board.

"As I have said very clearly, that is a process that is for the board to manage, and very improper for me to be involved in or to be aware of the details of her conversations with the board."

MacNeill said "it is for the board to manage their process under legal advice and to take correct steps under any employment law process".

"I don't have the capacity because I don't have the knowledge to comment on, you know, what her conversations were or weren't with the board in relation to that process," she added.

On Tuesday, the taoiseach said that the removal of O'Connor as chief executive is "fundamentally" a matter "for the [HSE] board and not for the minister".

"While the minister may be informed of the board's decision, the decision itself is one vested by law in the board," he added.

O'Connor previously said she would challenge her removal "as vigorously as possible" and "pursue every avenue available to me to vindicate my position and to protect my professional reputation".

She said she did not resign or voluntarily stand down.

Opposition politicians have voiced their concerns and the Irish Hospital Consultants Association has called on the HSE board to resign.

In an initial statement issued on Monday, the HSE said its board decided to end O'Connor's tenure as it was believed "to be in the best interests of the future operation of the organisation".

"The board would like to thank Anne for her service as CEO and for her many years in senior roles across the health service before that including as Chief Operations Officer throughout the Covid pandemic," the HSE added.

"Deputy Chief Executive Officer, Damien McCallion, has agreed to act as Chief Executive Officer in the interim pending the appointment of a new CEO."

articles.title: Israeli strike kills senior Hamas security official and family in Gaza City
articles.summary: Mohammed Abu al-Ouf, head of Hamas's internal security service in northern Gaza, was killed with his wife and two teenage daughters, doctors say.
articles.body:
An Israeli air strike in the Gaza Strip has killed a senior Hamas security official and three members of his family, according to local doctors and the Hamas-run interior ministry.

Mohammed Abu al-Ouf, 47, the head of Hamas's internal security service in northern Gaza, his wife and their two teenage daughters died when their apartment in Shati refugee camp in Gaza City was bombed at dawn, the ministry said.

The Israeli military said Abu al-Ouf was a "terrorist" and that he was eliminated "to remove the threat he posed".

On Tuesday, the overall commander of Hamas's internal security service was among 10 Palestinians reportedly killed in Israeli strikes.

Israeli air strike kills Hamas internal security chief in Gaza

Israeli attacks have turned Gaza into 'toxic wasteland', Oxfam says

Wednesday's strike in Shati caused extensive damage to the Abu al-Ouf family's apartment.

Photos showed the exterior wall and several interior walls were destroyed, with rubble and broken furniture left scattered across the floor.

An interior ministry statement said that Abu al-Ouf was killed along with his wife Noura, 41, and their daughters Yusra, 15, and Jana, 13.

It condemned the attack as a "heinous crime" and accused Israel of targeting security personnel in Gaza "in an effort to spread chaos within Palestinian society".

Hamas's internal security service is responsible for enforcing discipline, protecting the group's infrastructure and rooting out informants.

Israel's military said in a statement that Abu al-Ouf was a "significant figure" who had served as "a key source of expertise" in efforts to restrict Israeli counter-terrorism operations in Gaza.

"His elimination is a blow to the apparatus's leadership capabilities and follows yesterday's elimination of his commander," it added.

On Tuesday, an Israeli drone strike in western Gaza City killed Naeem Abu Nahel, the head of Hamas's internal security service.

He had only been in the position since September, when his predecessor was captured in a raid in Gaza City by Israeli special forces.

Near daily Israeli strikes continue in Gaza despite a ceasefire agreed in October last year.

At least 1,679 people have been killed in Gaza over the past 13 months, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN.

Israel says six of its soldiers have been killed in Gaza during the same period.

The Gaza war was triggered by the Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, when about 1,200 people were killed and 251 others were taken hostage.

Since then, more than 74,740 people have been killed in Israeli attacks in Gaza, the health ministry says.

articles.title: CM Suvendu orders police to deport 'illegal Muslim infiltrators', says Hindus fleeing Bangladesh are 'refugees'
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: West Bengal chief minister Suvendu Adhikari on Wednesday directed the state police to identify and trace, “one by one”, Muslim immigrants who
articles.body: NEW DELHI: West Bengal chief minister Suvendu Adhikari on Wednesday directed the state police to identify and trace, “one by one”, Muslim immigrants who had allegedly entered Cooch Behar district illegally from Bangladesh and send them back, while asserting that Hindus fleeing the neighbouring country should be treated as refugees and provided shelter.Addressing a programme during his visit to the district for the Rash Mela, Adhikari instructed Superintendent of Police Manish Joshi to take action against those he described as illegal infiltrators.“Illegal Muslim infiltrators from Bangladesh have to be identified and traced, one by one, in this district. They must be sent back through the same routes they used to enter. They have to be driven out,” he said.The chief minister, who also holds the Home portfolio, drew a distinction between Muslim immigrants he described as illegal entrants and Hindus arriving from Bangladesh.He said the latter had crossed the border to escape religious persecution and protect their lives.VIDEO | West Bengal: Chief Minister Suvendu Adhikari on Wednesday directed the police to trace Muslim immigrants who had allegedly entered the Cooch Behar district illegally from Bangladesh 'one by one,' and send them back.Addressing a programme during his visit to Cooch Behar for the Rash Mela, Adhikari told SP Manish Joshi that illegal Muslim immigrants from Bangladesh had no place in the state and must be sent back through the routes they had used to enter India."Illegal Muslim infiltrators from Bangladesh have to be identified and traced, one by one, in this district. They must be sent back through the same routes they used to enter. They have to be driven out," he said.The chief minister said Hindus coming from Bangladesh should not be treated as infiltrators, as they had crossed the border to escape religious persecution and save their lives."Those Hindus who have come from across the border are not infiltrators. They are refugees. They have come here to protect their religion and save their lives. They must be given shelter," he said.Adhikari, who also holds the Home portfolio, directed the state police and the Border Security Force (BSF) to work in close coordination to strengthen security along the international border.(Full video available on PTI Videos - Press Trust of India (@PTI_News) November 25, 2026“Those Hindus who have come from across the border are not infiltrators. They are refugees. They have come here to protect their religion and save their lives. They must be given shelter,” Adhikari said.Border security, smuggling and illegal madrasasAdhikari directed the state police and the Border Security Force (BSF) to work in close coordination to strengthen security along the international border.He said the state government had provided the necessary land to the BSF for border infrastructure and fencing, and called for all forms of smuggling to be stopped once the fencing work was completed.The chief minister also asked the police to crack down on what he described as illegal madrasas in border areas, as well as ganja cultivation, fake currency circulation and drug trafficking.“Illegal madrasas, ganja cultivation, fake currency and narcotics trafficking along the border must be stopped,” he said.Cooch Behar shares a sensitive border with Bangladesh, with illegal immigration and smuggling remaining prominent issues in the region's political discourse.Warning over crimes against women, cow slaughterAdhikari also warned that his government would take strict action against violence against women. He felicitated members of 'Durga Bahini', a specially trained women police force, and handed over 30 scooters to its personnel to improve their field presence.“The government will not tolerate any violence against women. Strict action will be taken at all times. If anyone raises a finger against even one of my sisters or daughters, that finger must be broken,” he said.He further instructed the police to strictly enforce the provisions of the West Bengal Animal Slaughter Control Act, 1950.“Police must look into the 1950 law. There should be no raising of hands against 'Gau Mata'. I am making this absolutely clear,” the chief minister said.Adhikari had said on Monday that his government would introduce a Bill in the state Assembly to curb indiscriminate cow slaughter.Recalls alleged attack on convoyThe chief minister also referred to an alleged attack on his convoy in the Khagrabari Chowpathi area of Cooch Behar on August 5, 2025, when he was the Leader of the Opposition. He claimed that petrol had been poured on his vehicle during the incident.The investigation was reopened after he became chief minister, leading to several arrests.“I have endured a lot. Petrol was poured on my car in Khagrabari. I have all the photographs of the incident carefully preserved,” he said.Adhikari added, “Development will continue, but accountability will also be ensured (Unnayan-o Hobe, Hisaab-o Hobe).”Several state ministers and BJP MLAs attended the programme. The chief minister asked them to ensure that government schemes reached people across all sections of society. He also outlined a vision of transforming villages into towns and towns into metropolitan centres in Cooch Behar.Separately, speaking to reporters on the sidelines of the Rash Mela, Adhikari declined to elaborate on his earlier claim that former President Pranab Mukherjee had advised him to leave the Trinamool Congress (TMC) and align with Prime Minister Narendra Modi to advance independently in politics.Adhikari described Mukherjee as a “great personality” and said he did not want any unnecessary discussion about the late Congress leader.Adhikari had made the claim at an Economic Times event in Kolkata on Tuesday, recalling that Mukherjee had advised him that he would remain an “employee” under the TMC leadership if he continued in the party.He had quoted Mukherjee as saying, “If you want to remain an employee, stay with her. articles.title: California braces for major flooding as record-breaking high tides hit coast; 20-30ft waves raise alarm
articles.summary: California is bracing for coastal flooding as a second day of record-breaking high tides brings dangerously large waves to the US West Coast, raising
articles.body: California is bracing for coastal flooding as a second day of record-breaking high tides brings dangerously large waves to the US West Coast, raising concerns over road closures, beach safety and travel disruptions during the busy Thanksgiving holiday week.The National Weather Service (NWS) has warned of waves reaching 20-30 feet in parts of the coast, while officials have advised residents and visitors to stay away from beaches and low-lying areas. Several cities have also announced beach closures amid fears of powerful surf and dangerous rip currents.According to The Guardian, California officials have been preparing for weeks for the possibility of flooding during one of the busiest travel periods of the year. San Francisco International Airport, located on low-lying coastal land, has been a particular concern. At least three airlines have offered passengers free changes to trips passing through the airport on Wednesday.The airport said it had not experienced any flooding impacts on Tuesday. The peak of the seasonal high tides, known as "king tides", is expected along the California coast on Wednesday morning.Waves could reach 30 feet, officials warnThe NWS has forecast breaking waves of 20-25 feet in northern California and 20-30 feet around San Francisco. Along the central coast, between San Francisco and Los Angeles, waves could reach 12-22 feet, accompanied by dangerous rip currents.Cities including Santa Cruz, Monterey and Carmel-by-the-Sea have announced beach closures, citing the risk posed by the forecast conditions. Officials have also warned of flooding on low-lying roads near beaches and bays, while several road closures are possible in the San Francisco Bay Area.The San Luis Obispo County Office of Emergency Services has urged people visiting the coast to watch the tides from a safe distance. The county's fire department warned that powerful waves can sweep people into the ocean, putting both visitors and emergency responders at risk.California Governor Gavin Newsom said the state had taken early steps to prepare for the weather threat, including strengthening flood defences, positioning emergency supplies and coordinating with local emergency crews. He also urged residents to exercise caution while travelling for Thanksgiving.El Niño adds to coastal flooding concernsThe flooding threat is linked to a combination of factors, including unusually high Pacific Ocean water levels, seasonal king tides and the influence of a strong El Niño weather pattern.Weather experts have warned that the danger could increase if heavy rain and strong winds from a winter storm coincide with peak high tides, potentially worsening coastal flooding.California appears to have avoided the worst-case scenario during the November king tide period so far. However, another round of exceptionally high tides is expected around December 23-25, followed by a further peak in late January, when winter storms could pose additional risks.You use AI every day. articles.title: An 84-year-old Arkansas widow returned to work after her husband's death to pay medical bills; a friend's fundraiser has now raised over $31,000 and helped her finally retire after years of financial strain
articles.summary: Sue Webb, an 84-year-old Arkansas widow, returns to work after her husband's death to settle medical bills, but a friend's fundraiser has raised over $31,000, allowing her to finally retire and focus on her health.
articles.body: After spending years caring for her husband through serious illness, Sue Webb expected to spend her retirement years at home. Instead, the Arkansas widow found herself returning to work to deal with the medical debt left behind after his death. Now, a fundraiser organised by a friend has raised more than $31,000, helping her finally step away from her job.Webb, 84, spent 50 years married to her husband, Gene, a Korean War veteran. She retired early from her career in the financial sector to become his full-time caregiver after he was diagnosed with Alzheimer's disease and later brain cancer.His treatment and long-term care, however, placed a heavy financial burden on the couple. Their retirement savings were used to cover medical expenses and nursing home costs, leaving Webb with outstanding bills after his death in 2017.With little money left to support herself, she returned to work at the Department of Veterans Affairs (VA), where she is involved in palliative care and patient education.In an interview with WFMY News 2, Webb said she had to continue working to manage her expenses and deal with the debt accumulated during her husband's illness.Why did Sue Webb return to work after her husband's death?Webb had spent 35 years working full-time in the financial sector before leaving her job to care for Gene. His health deteriorated after he developed Alzheimer's disease and brain cancer, eventually requiring nursing home care, according to WFMY News 2.The cost of looking after him consumed the savings the couple had built over their years together. After his death, Webb was left with medical and long-term care bills that she continued to pay while trying to support herself.Her GoFundMe page describes how she continued working into her eighties despite facing health challenges of her own. When asked why she had not retired, Webb reportedly gave a simple answer: "so I can live."Her circumstances prompted her friend, Tina Alderson, to step in and organise a fundraiser to help clear the financial burden and allow Webb to focus on her health.Alderson explained that Webb had used both her own and her husband's retirement savings to pay for his treatment and care. Once he died, she had little choice but to return to work to rebuild her finances and settle the outstanding expenses.GoFundMe campaign raised more than $31,000The fundraising campaign initially struggled to attract significant attention. However, it gained momentum after content creator Samuel Weidenhofer came across Webb's story and shared it with his large social media following.Weidenhofer was running an initiative called '50 Veterans, 50 Days, 50 States', aimed at supporting veterans and their families across the United States. Webb was selected to represent Arkansas as part of the campaign.Alderson said the initiative helped bring wider attention to Webb's financial situation and encouraged people to contribute.The GoFundMe campaign has since collected more than $31,000, providing Webb with financial relief after years of paying off her husband's medical expenses.According to WFMY News 2, the donations have already helped her clear several costs, including the outstanding payment on her car.Webb retired in May after being diagnosed with a heart condition. The financial support has allowed her to step away from work after continuing her job well beyond the usual retirement age.The donations have given Webb an opportunity to focus on her own well-being after years spent caring for her husband and managing the financial consequences of his illness.Her GoFundMe page describes her as someone who continued to show kindness to others despite facing personal and health-related difficulties. It also highlights her work in palliative care and patient education, where she supported people going through difficult medical circumstances.Speaking about the response to the fundraiser, Webb thanked everyone who contributed to helping her retire."I just want to thank everyone that did donate. Thank you from the bottom of my heart," she told WFMY News 2. "It means everything to me."You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: US Army detonates toxic lead explosives in Iowa amid health concerns
articles.summary: The US Army destroys nearly 4,500kg of lead azide amid fears of toxic fallout affecting residents, farms and livestock.
articles.body:
A large stockpile of lead-rich explosives in the Midwestern state of Iowa has been destroyed in controlled detonations by the United States Army, ending a brief legal battle spurred by concerns that toxic dust from the fallout would endanger residents, livestock and farmland.

Video showed that the nearly 4,500kg (10,000lb) of lead azide – a highly volatile, lead-based explosive that has been used in military munitions since World War I – was detonated in two successive open-air detonations on Wednesday at around 9am (15:00 GMT).

Environmental groups have raised concerns that the explosions would release particles that could eventually land on homes, crops and livestock far beyond the detonation site, potentially travelling more than 160km (100 miles).

Before the detonations at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant, outgoing Republican Governor Kim Reynolds declared a disaster emergency across three counties in southeastern Iowa – Des Moines, Lee and Van Buren – activating state and county emergency response plans.

Shortly before the controlled detonations, Assistant Secretary of the Army Jordan Gillis appeared in a video on X, discussing the decision behind the detonation and explaining how the Army is attempting to mitigate the particles released. “The choice that we faced here was between a spontaneous, uncontrolled detonation of dangerous material or a controlled detonation where we could choose the time and place to optimize the conditions to deliver the best result – not just for our operation but for the safety of the public,” Gillis said.

Revised wind projections released by the Army on Tuesday showed that airborne lead particles would shift southwest into northeast Missouri, prompting health officials there to advise residents 8km to 32km (5 to 20 miles) southwest of the plant to shelter indoors with windows and doors shut until an all-clear is issued.

A looming hazard for communities under strain

Amid a groundswell of concern over the prospect of toxic lead fallout, some residents have warned of the added burden the operation could place on communities already contending with chronic economic pressures, including a shortage of affordable housing, rising food costs and stretched local services.

The detonation’s impact will be felt across Des Moines County, which covers the city of Burlington and the rural community of Middletown, immediately adjacent to the ammunition plant.

Home to about 38,000 Iowans, the county had 38 percent of its households below the Asset Limited, Income Constrained, Employed (ALICE) threshold in 2024, according to the latest figures published by United for ALICE, a national research initiative.

“We shouldn’t have to experience an environmental disaster to become worthy of national attention or investment,” Megan Brincks, chairwoman of the Burlington Homelessness Task Force, told Al Jazeera.

Brincks, a Burlington resident who previously worked in the ammunition plant’s chemistry laboratory, stressed that the Army’s shelter-in-place orders cannot suspend the daily obligations of those whose work keeps the community running.

“Our food-insecure families will still need food tomorrow,” Brincks said, adding: “People experiencing homelessness will still need shelter. Individuals will still need transportation to medical appointments.”

“Unfortunately, the world doesn’t stop spinning because this is happening in our back yard.”

The blasts rocked one of southeastern Iowa’s most heavily cultivated stretches of land in a state that ranks second only to California in agricultural output value.

According to the US Department of Agriculture (USDA), Iowa is a leading producer of corn and soya beans and ranks first in the country in commercial red meat and egg production.

Across Des Moines County, about 648 farms span nearly 60,300 hectares (149,000 acres), including more than 49,775 hectares (123,000 acres) of cropland.

On Tuesday, Richard Fordyce, an undersecretary at the USDA, said the agency and the Iowa Department of Agriculture and Land Stewardship estimated that about 350 farms across Iowa and Missouri could lie within the projected plume area.

The prospect has stoked alarm over the risk of lead leaching into soil and groundwater, compromising crops and livestock and jeopardising the livelihoods of the farmers whose land underpins a vital part of the country’s food supply.

Will Sander, an associate professor of preventive medicine and public health at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, said much of Iowa’s corn and soya bean harvest has already been completed, reducing the likelihood of acute exposure to this season’s crops.

Cattle producers, he said, should cover feed and water supplies where possible to limit animals’ ingestion of lead dust even if they cannot bring their herds under shelter.

“The acute exposure is the biggest risk in this situation, … that lead will not have dispersed and diluted into the environment,” Sander told Al Jazeera.

“For [these] farmers, land is their currency,” Eri Saikawa, a professor of environmental sciences at Emory University, said. “It is not acceptable that their livelihood is impacted this way. It also impacts all of us who rely on these farmers and their crops.”

articles.title: Eight Pennsylvania relatives challenged a will naming a second cousin as sole heir after their uncle died in 2014; 12 years later, an appeals court upheld $598,686 in fees for the lawyer who defeated the disputed will
articles.summary: A Pennsylvania inheritance fight that started after a man died in 2014 has reached another milestone.
articles.body: A Pennsylvania inheritance fight that started after a man died in 2014 has reached another milestone. An appeals court upheld a $598,686 payment to the lawyer who helped eight relatives overturn a disputed will. The case involved a second cousin named as the sole heir, claims that the will was forged, and a long battle over how much the family's lawyer should be paid. The Pennsylvania Superior Court backed an October 2025 order granting lawyer Richard P. Joseph $598,686.34 in legal fees and costs. The ruling, released on 24 November 2026, turned down Joseph's challenge to the payout amount and his claim that the judge handling the fee dispute was biased and should have stepped aside.The decision means the legal-fee payment stands, ending another chapter of this long estate battle. The original court fight over the will had already declared the disputed paper invalid, letting the dead man's eight nieces and nephews inherit his money under Pennsylvania laws for people who die without a valid will. According to the court's memorandum, the fight began after John J. Thomas died on 12 October 2014. His second cousin, Timothy Ungarean, showed a paper dated 7 July 2014 that named him as the sole heir to Thomas's estate. The eight surviving nieces and nephews fought the paper in court, claiming it was forged.Second cousin named sole beneficiary in disputed willThomas died leaving eight nieces and nephews: Theresa A. Thomas, Carol L. Thomas, Norman J. Thomas, Anna Marie Rheingrover, David J. George, Alex C. George, Charles T. George, and James H. George Jr. On 23 October 2014, the Beaver County Register of Wills accepted the paper as valid and gave Ungarean official permission to manage the estate under that will. The eight relatives, represented by Joseph, appealed that decision. They challenged the paper's validity and asked the court to take away Ungarean's power to run the estate.A trial without a jury started in October 2018 and lasted until January 2019. Judge Paul F. Lutty ruled that the will dated 7 July 2014 was invalid. He also found that other papers said to be signed by Thomas on that same day were invalid. Because of this, the court cancelled Ungarean's authority to manage the estate and ruled that Thomas died without a valid will. His money and property would go to his legal heirs instead of Ungarean. Ungarean appealed, but the Pennsylvania Superior Court backed the trial ruling on 6 March 2020. According to the court's account, Joseph also represented the eight relatives during that appeal.Lawyer seeks 40% of estate under fee agreementOnce the fight over the will ended, Joseph asked to be paid for his legal work based on a deal signed with the relatives in December 2014. That paper, called a Power of Attorney, set up a payment plan based on winning the case. Under the deal, Joseph would get 33⅓% of any settlement reached. That share would rise to 40% of a court award or settlement after evidence gathering ended and the court ruled on early motions that did not close the case. The deal also required the relatives to pay court costs and expenses ahead of time. The relatives were asked to put $15,000 into Joseph's holding account, with more money needed if that ran out. The agreement also covered appeal costs if the relatives lost at trial and chose to fight the ruling. Joseph later argued that he should get 40% of the entire estate, including money recovered later on. This sparked a new fight over what the fee deal meant and how much money he could claim. In September 2023, the Orphans' Court first awarded Joseph $851,505, plus a 40% share in other estate assets. The people managing the estate challenged that order, saying the payout was about 55% of the cash held in the account and that the wording might let Joseph demand even more.Appeals court sends fee dispute back for reviewThe estate appealed the first fee award, and the Superior Court issued a new ruling on 24 October 2024. It agreed Joseph earned a 40% share, but found the contract did not clearly explain how to calculate that percentage. The court ruled the fee had to be based on the net cash left in the holding account to be shared among the heirs. It also decided Joseph could not charge extra fees for defending the relatives during Ungarean's appeal, because the contract only covered appeal costs if the family lost at trial and Joseph appealed for them. The judges also ordered that money the relatives had already paid up front for expenses must be subtracted when figuring out his fee. They cancelled the earlier orders and sent the case back to the Orphans' Court for a new hearing. The case then went to Judge Michael F. Marmo after Judge Lutty retired. A hearing to review evidence was set for 21 March 2025.Lawyer's absence leads to another court disputeJoseph skipped the March 2025 hearing. According to the court's memorandum, he had asked Judge Marmo's office for a 120-day delay due to health issues tied to long COVID-19. The judge's staff turned down the delay because the case had dragged on so long, though they let Joseph join by video. Court secretary Mindy Frohlich later testified that she emailed him on 14 March 2025 to say the hearing would happen as planned and gave him call-in details. Joseph insisted he was too sick to take part and questioned whether the judge was fair. He also complained about how settlement talks were handled and claimed lawyers for the estate had conflicts of interest. During a phone call with the court on 21 March, Joseph and Judge Marmo had a heated argument. Joseph then filed a formal request on 5 May 2025 asking the judge to step down from the case.That request was denied after a hearing on 16 July. A second hearing to review evidence on the legal fees happened on 15 August 2025. On 30 October 2025, the Orphans' Court awarded Joseph $598,686.34. That sum included 40% of the $1,478,001.94 net holding balance, plus $42,972.65 for expenses, minus $35,487.09 the relatives had already paid up front. The court did not give him a legal claim against the estate's assets to guarantee payment. Joseph appealed on 10 November 2025, fighting the fee math and arguing Judge Marmo should have stepped aside.Superior Court rejects appeal and upholds paymentThe Pennsylvania Superior Court found that Joseph failed to turn in a key record needed to review the fee math. The written record of the 15 August 2025 hearing was missing from the official court file. The judges explained it was Joseph's job to make sure the needed hearing records were included. Without that transcript, they could not review the facts used to figure out his pay, so his challenge to the amount was dropped. The court also rejected his claims that the judge was biased. It noted Judge Marmo let Joseph share his side, kept the hearing record open, and set up another chance for him to question witnesses and show evidence.The appeals court said the judge's stern words during the hearings did not prove bias or stop Joseph from getting a fair hearing. It found no misuse of power in the decision to turn down his request for a new judge. In its memorandum filed on 24 November 2026, the Superior Court upheld the Orphans' Court order. The ruling in In Re: Estate of John J. Thomas, docket number 1457 WDA 2025, keeps the $598,686.34 legal-fee payout in place. The ruling does not reopen the original fight over the will. articles.title: South Africa court repeals ‘farmgate’ impeachment threat against Ramaphosa
articles.summary: The ruling hands the president a political reprieve by removing a finding that had exposed him to possible impeachment.
articles.body:
South African President Cyril Ramaphosa has won a court bid challenging an independent panel’s report that had paved the way for his possible impeachment over misconduct allegations linked to a burglary-turned-political scandal called “Farmgate”.

The Western Cape High Court on Wednesday declared unlawful the 2022 findings of an independent parliamentary panel that accused Ramaphosa of a conflict of interest over the origin of large amounts of cash stolen from a sofa at his ranch in 2020.

The ruling hands Ramaphosa a political reprieve by removing a finding that had exposed him to possible impeachment at a vulnerable moment for him and his African National Congress (ANC) party.

“The court found that the panel fundamentally misconstrued its functions,” Judge Nolwazi Mabindla-Boqwana said, reading the court’s unanimous decision.

“The ‌panel went beyond its lawful remit, asked itself wrong questions and made several material errors of law.”

Ramaphosa “notes” and “will study” the court’s judgement relating to his Phala Phala game farm, the president’s office said in a statement.

“In seeking the judicial review, President Ramaphosa exercised a constitutional right,” the statement read. “In line with his respect for the rule of law including judicial independence, President Ramaphosa will study the decision of the court.”

The theft came to light after a former intelligence boss reported to the police that Ramaphosa had allegedly sought to cover up a theft of millions of US dollars in cash at his farm, initially claiming it was about $4m.

Ramaphosa has always denied wrongdoing and said the $580,000 stolen at his farm ⁠was money from the sale of buffaloes.

But the episode raised questions about ⁠why he had so much cash stuffed in furniture.

The 2022 report said the president failed to report the theft through proper channels, violated the constitution regarding paid work from his farm and directed presidential security to do police work.

The African Transformation Movement party, which is in favour of Ramaphosa’s impeachment, criticised the ruling.

The matter has been embarrassing for a ⁠leader who came to power promising to fight corruption and clean up the image of the former liberation movement.

The ANC won about 31 percent of the vote in this month’s local elections, its worst-ever such result, extending a decline that saw it lose its national parliamentary majority in 2024 for the first time since the end of apartheid and beginning of democracy.

The Constitutional Court revived impeachment proceedings against the president in ⁠May.

It found that a 2022 parliamentary vote to stop the process ⁠was invalid and parliament should set up an impeachment inquiry.

The Western Cape High Court in July temporarily halted the inquiry pending the outcome of Wednesday’s ruling.

Ramaphosa, 74, has been head of state since 2018, and his second presidential ‌term ‌is to end in 2029. The ANC is due to elect its next leader next year when Ramaphosa will step down after two five-year terms as party leader.

articles.title: Poundland collapses putting 11,000 jobs at risk
articles.summary: The discount chain has fallen into administration after its owners failed to find a buyer.
articles.body:
Poundland has collapsed into administration, putting 11,000 jobs at risk, after its owners failed to find a buyer to keep it in business.

The retailer's shops and distribution centres will remain open and continue to trade during the administration process with the business likely to be broken up and some of its stores sold off to rival retailers.

Poundland's US owners held talks with several bidders over a last-minute rescue deal, but no agreement was reached.

Poundland boss Barry Williams said in a note to staff that the board had "no alternative but to take this decision", but was making it with "sincere sadness and intense regret".

He said the US owners Gordon Brothers had removed "all borrowing facilities and access to our bank accounts" on 27 October, and adequate funds had not been released since then to keep the business solvent.

"Under these circumstances, it is impossible for the board of directors to see how Poundland can continue to operate as a going concern," he added.

Kelvin Blake, 62, who has worked for the firm for 25 years, and whose partner has been there 29 years, said he was feeling "down, depressed", and because of his age, feared he would not find a job elsewhere.

"We didn't want it, but it's come so now we've just got to face it and see what the future holds.

"My income's gone," he added. "Obviously, we'll be working until we're told to leave."

Prime Minister Andy Burnham said Poundland was "part of the fabric of high streets and communities up and down the country".

He said the news of it going into administration just weeks before Christmas would be "deeply concerning for workers and their families".

He added: "While it is worrying, going into administration does give other potential buyers the opportunity to engage and we will work hard with all the relevant parties to ensure the best possible outcome."

Alix Partners, which has been appointed as administrator, said they would look at all options for the business, "including sales of the business and its assets, either in whole or part".

"We appreciate this is a deeply concerning time for all involved - customers, suppliers and, in particular, Poundland colleagues," they said.

Gordon Brothers has been criticised over how it handled a potential sale of Poundland, with accusations the investment firm hoped to profit from selling off the chain's 600 shops and stock piecemeal after running it into the ground.

Gordon Brothers, which specialises in buying and restructuring distressed companies, has denied such claims.

On the funding question, Gordon Brothers said it had loaned the firm £85m over a year to help save it from insolvency.

But insiders critical of the US firm have said it stands to make its loans back and more from the insolvency process.

Previously, Gordon Brothers netted millions from liquidating the stock of fashion retailer LK Bennett, and in insolvency fees.

Labour MP Liam Byrne told the BBC the House of Commons' Business, Innovation, Science and Trade Committee will recall Gordon Brothers before Parliament - two weeks after Gordon Brothers representatives last appeared at the committee to answer questions about Poundland, and where MPs said they were "deeply concerned" about the business.

Byrne said: "I am really worried that a 'greed is good' approach to business by its owners has forced [Poundland] into an administration."

He added the committee wants to know "how much money they're ripping out and crucially, how do we make sure, as a country, that we don't have this kind of scenario unfold again".

Gordon Brothers met Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds on Monday to update him on the progress.

The firm said on Wednesday that despite the Poundland management bringing about a turnaround over the past year, the firm was "still vulnerable" to inflation and any downturn in sales or profit margin, and it had faced "several years of instability".

A spokesperson added the firm's "thoughts are with Poundland colleagues".

It said it had stepped in to take over the retailer in 2025 when it was struggling, and when "no-one else was willing to finance the business".

One of the central stumbling blocks in negotiations to keep the business afloat was a shareholder loan Gordon Brothers inherited when it bought the business for less than £1 last year.

Gordon Brothers was owed £22.5m of that loan, while the previous owner Pepco was owed £7.5m.

Gordon Brothers rejected various offers to buy the business as a going concern with deals to pay off that loan.

Irish firm Martin Property Group offered to pay off £5m of the loan up front, and defer the rest of the payments to 2030.

London-based Xyra group offered £12.5m up front but ran out of time to get a deal over the line.

German investment firm Zachert Private Equity is also understood to have made a late offer.

The crisis at Poundland really came to a head over the past few weeks after Gordon Brothers restricted access to funds for day-to-day operations.

This meant that stock at the retailer was not being replenished at the necessary pace in the vital run-up to the festive period.

articles.title: Dublin M50: Four youths charged over wrong-way collision
articles.summary: Dublin M50: Four youths have been charged in connection with a crash in which a man in his 20s was seriously injured.
articles.body:
Four youths have been charged in connection with a crash on Dublin's M50 in which a man in his 20s was seriously injured.

A vehicle travelling the wrong way collided head-on with his car near junction 12 at Firhouse on 9 August.

Seven youths were arrested by gardaí (Irish police) in Tallaght on Wednesday morning. Three remain in custody.

The four charged are due to appear in court in Dublin on Wednesday.

Three are due before the Children's Court in Smithfield, while the fourth is due before the District Court at the Criminal Courts of Justice.

Gardaí said the vehicle was travelling north on the motorway's southbound carriageway and was driving down an entry slip road when the collision happened.

They said they remain in contact with the injured driver and have made him aware of developments in the investigation.

articles.title: Trump’s accounts traded Nvidia shares 44 times this year, records show
articles.summary: A review of the US president's financial disclosures shows Donald Trump's investment portfolios have regularly traded shares in the tech giant.
articles.body:
Donald Trump's investment portfolios have bought or sold shares in chipmaker Nvidia at least 44 times this year, a review of the US president's financial disclosures shows.

Trump's most recent public declarations of his investment trading show that between January and September the portfolios purchased between $5.2m and $17m (£4m and £13m) in Nvidia stock - and sold between $4.4m and $12m. His portfolios held between $12.5m and $58m of Nvidia shares at the end of 2025.

Financial disclosures to the Office of Government Ethics report a low and high range of transaction values, so a more precise analysis of how much Nvidia stock was traded is not possible.

The period of recent turmoil at Nvidia and volatility in its share price is not covered by the disclosures. In the last two weeks, co-founder and chief executive Jensen Huang resigned and then Trump played a significant part in his reinstatement.

The White House has said that Trump's stock and bond portfolio is independently managed by third parties and neither he nor his family "has any ability to direct, influence or provide input regarding how the portfolio is invested or when investments are bought or sold".

Huang resigned on 12 November after reports of extramarital affairs, including with one woman who has alleged ties to Chinese intelligence. Nvidia's share price dived following news of his resignation.

But on Monday Nvidia's board announced the 63-year-old was being reinstated as CEO.

Trump told US media he had "made the deal" to "convince" the tech giant's board to bring Huang back. The board said it had "received input from senior levels of the United States government" that he posed "no national security risk".

Nvidia's share price surged 31% on Monday following Huang's return. About $1tn (£763bn) was added to Nvidia's market value, but the company's shares are still trading below their value before reports of Huang's alleged affairs began to circulate.

However, concerns remain among both Republican and Democratic politicians about Huang's actions and Nvidia's compliance with US controls over the export of advanced computer chips to China, as well as Trump's involvement in getting him reappointed as CEO.

Nvidia's chip technology and investments have been critical to the growth of the artificial intelligence (AI) industry , leading to it becoming one of the world's most valuable companies.

The firm now represents more than 6% of the S&P 500 share index, according to State Street financial services. This makes it the second most valuable company on the index after Apple, whose shares Trump's accounts also frequently trade.

Nvidia also ranks highly in many global indices, meaning that investment accounts held around the world, including pensions, are likely to include its shares.

Our analysis of Trump's Nvidia trades does not include other investment products held by him which may include its shares.

Trump made at least $2.2bn (£1.7bn) from a variety of investments and commercial activities, according to the financial disclosure report for the first year of Trump's second term.

Barbara Perry, a presidential historian at the University of Virginia's Miller Center, told the BBC there is "no precedent for this," adding: "It's beyond anything we've ever seen in the presidency."

articles.title: Libyans pledge to retaliate after Ukraine strikes Russian warship near Benghazi, killing 2 soldiers
articles.summary: The Libyan National Army mourns two soldiers who died Tuesday from a Ukrainian drone strike on a Russian warship in Benghazi, vowing retaliation.
articles.body: The Libyan National Army (LNA) has vowed to retaliate after a Ukrainian drone attack on a Russian warship moored at a Benghazi port killed two Libyan soldiers. "With deep sadness and sorrow, and with hearts believing in the decree and destiny of Allah, the General Command of the Libyan Arab Armed Forces mourns two of its heroic sons belonging to the Naval Forces General Staff," the LNA wrote in a Facebook post on Tuesday. Calling the Ukrainian attack "sinful aggression," the LNA also quoted the Quran, writing, "And those who have wronged are going to know to what [kind of] return they will be returned." RUSSIA WARNS OF 'PREVENTIVE NUCLEAR ATTACK' AS MEDVEDEV CLAIMS UKRAINE, NATO CROSSED LINE The LNA said the soldiers, identified as Al-Taher Abdullah al-Sadiq and Lieutenant Ali Mohammed al-Said, died Tuesday from injuries sustained during the Sunday attack. Libya's eastern government, the Government of National Stability, was joined by the country's U.N.-recognized western government, the Government of National Unity, based in the capital, Tripoli, in criticizing the attack. US CALLS TURKEY-LIBYA MARITIME DEAL 'UNHELPFUL AND PROVOCATIVE' AMID REGIONAL BACKLASH "The Ministry of Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation of the Government of National Unity has expressed its condemnation and denunciation of statements made by the Ukrainian President regarding the execution of military operations targeting Russian naval vessels in the vicinity of the city of Benghazi," the Ministry wrote in a statement. The Tripoli-based government also denied accusations that the Ukrainian attack was launched from Libyan territorial waters. FRENCH TROOPS SECRETLY DEPLOYED INSIDE UKRAINE AS EX-NATO CHIEF PRAISES MACRON'S 'GUTS' "The Ministry categorically rejects the conduct of any foreign military operations within Libyan territory or its territorial waters," it added. Despite the denial, Libya's eastern government requested an investigation into the possibility that the drone strike was launched from Western Libya, citing information that Ukrainian military could be present in "areas around Misrata, Zawiya and other potential locations," according to news outlet Al Arabiya. NATO FIGHTER JET CLEARED TO SHOOT DOWN RUSSIAN MISSILE OVER POLAND AS WARSAW PUSHES FOR US TROOPS Western Libya's government criticized the Benghazi-based eastern government for hosting Russian ships in the first place. "Hosting illicit foreign forces and granting them access to national facilities invites the spillover of external conflicts into the country," Tripoli said, according to Al Arabiya. The Benghazi-based LNA is the military arm of Libya's eastern government, one half of the ruling party in the North African nation. Following the fall of former Libyan dictator Muammar Qadaffi, rivaling power factions made claims on ruling the nation. The United Nations-backed western government counts the U.S. and European Union among its supporters. The eastern government is broadly aligned with Russia and is not formally recognized by the U.N. Russia supported Libya's vow for revenge. "Well, certainly, no state will leave an attempt on the lives of its servicemen unpunished," Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said in a video. Ukraine, while confirming the strike, claimed it was self-defense. "Ukraine respects the sovereignty and territorial integrity of Libya. We emphasize that Ukraine's actions are aimed at countering Russian armed aggression and are not intended to harm Libya or its people," Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said in a message posted to Telegram. Sybiha also said that the ships it attacked — Russian naval vessels and cargo ships transporting military equipment — were valid military targets as defined by the United Nations Charter's Article 51. "Ukraine is not 'dragging' anyone into the war or 'transferring' the war anywhere," Sybiha added. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy also confirmed a separate drone strike on a Russian ship in the Gulf of Finland on Saturday. articles.title: Pre-Thanksgiving flight to Chicago disrupted when unruly passenger rushes toward airplane door
articles.summary: An American Airlines flight to Chicago diverted to Phoenix, Arizona, after an unruly passenger allegedly tried to pry open an aircraft door mid-flight.
articles.body: A Chicago-bound American Airlines flight had to divert to Phoenix, Arizona, on Wednesday, after an unruly passenger allegedly attempted to pry open an aircraft door, the Federal Aviation Administration confirmed. The flight landed safely at Phoenix Sky Harbor International Airport around 1 a.m. local time Wednesday, Nov. 25, after the crew reported a passenger disturbance on board, the FAA told Fox News Digital in a statement. The flight, which originated in San Diego, once again headed for its destination of Chicago O’Hare International Airport after the unruly passenger was removed, according to the FAA and American Airlines. ENGINE FAILURE FORCES SEN ASHLEY MOODY’S AMERICAN AIRLINES FLIGHT TO DIVERT FOR EMERGENCY LANDING "American Airlines flight 1494 diverted to Phoenix (PHX) due to a disruptive customer. Upon arrival, law enforcement met the aircraft and assisted with deplaning the customer before the flight continued to its destination," the airline told Fox News Digital in a statement. "The safety and security of our customers and team members is our top priority. We thank our team members for their professionalism and our customers for their assistance and understanding," the statement concluded. FLIGHT PASSENGER YELLS, 'I WANT OFF,' CALLS CREW 'IDIOTS' AND YANKS OPEN EMERGENCY EXIT DOOR Phoenix police told Fox News Digital the passenger left his assigned seat and moved to the front of the aircraft. After repeatedly refusing crew instructions to sit down, the passenger reportedly attempted to manipulate a cabin door while the plane flew over the California-Arizona border. RETIRED POLICE CHIEF HELPS SUBDUE PASSENGER AFTER ALLEGED MIDAIR OUTBURST OVER ALCOHOL CUTOFF Crew members, assisted by other passengers, subdued and restrained the man until the Phoenix landing, Phoenix Police told Fox News Digital in a statement. The passenger sustained a minor injury but no other passengers or crew members were harmed, police said. TWICE-DEPORTED ILLEGAL IMMIGRANT ACCUSED OF TRYING TO STORM UNITED COCKPIT, THREATENING BOMB: DHS The FAA has received reports of more than 1,500 unruly passenger incidents so far in 2026, the FAA told Fox News Digital in a statement. A passenger who assaults, threatens, intimidates or interferes with airline crew members can incur civil penalties up to $43,658 per violation. articles.title: The County Tyrone town was announced as one location for the inaugural UK Town of Culture 2028, with the chance to win £3m.
articles.summary: UK Town of Culture: Strabane bid withdrawn over 'potential disaster for community relations'
articles.body:
A competition that is supposed to celebrate local towns has been rejected by a council after it caused "great division" over its UK title.

The mainly-nationalist town of Strabane in County Tyrone was announced as one of the 15 locations for the inaugural UK Town of Culture 2028, with the chance to win £3m.

However, the local council voted not to go ahead with the bid on Wednesday with one councillor claiming it "has the potential to be a disaster for Strabane - for community relations".

The motion, which was put forward by independent councillors, was backed by the Social Democratic and Labour Party (SDLP) and Sinn Féin.

The council has to date spent around £40,000 on the bid.

A report prepared for councillors said that money had come from a £60,000 Department for Culture, Media and Sport (DCMS) grant, and would need to be repaid if the bid did not make it to the final submission stage.

Independent Paul Gallagher, who had previously expressed concerns about the town's entry in the competition, said it had "caused great division in Strabane town".

He said there was widespread concerns about the competition's UK title.

"If it was to go forward it would create a major distrust in this council among the residents of Strabane," said Gallagher.

Strabane, he said, would become "a very uncomfortable place" if the bid was progressed, adding there was the potential for protests in the town.

The overall Town of Culture winner UK Town of Culture 2028 will receive £3m to develop a year-long programme of cultural celebrations while the other two finalists will each receive £250,000.

Unionists on Derry City and Strabane District Council said it was disappointing the bid was not being progressed to a final submission stage.

There is a deadline of 30 November for final bid submissions.

Sinn Féin councillor Brian Harte said they were backing the motion after "consulting with and listening to representations from many people within the local community".

"We must acknowledge that the UK branding of this competition has prevented a large section of the local community and key groups from identifying with or participating in the bid," he said.

He said the debate around the branding had "become toxic in recent months", adding council officials working on the bid had been subjected some abuse, particularly online.

SDLP councillor Catherine McDaid said local concerns "need to be taken seriously".

"A cultural initiative should bring people together," she said.

"The priority now has to be to work on what has already been completed and looking into fresh opportunities for Strabane, shaped by what local people want and need, and grounded in their support," she said.

Ulster Unionist councillor Derek Hussey said it was "remiss" not to pursue with the bid.

Strabane and its people, he said, were being denied a similar opportunity to that of Derry which was the inaugural UK City of Culture in 2013.

Staying in the competition, he said, could "only be to the social and economic wellbeing of residents, business and visitors, long term as has been proved previously with the city's experience of having had the title of UK City of Culture," he said.

The Democratic Unionist Party's Keith Kerrigan said it was disappointing that at a time of wider investment in Strabane, the potential of a further £3m was being taken away.

"It is disappointing but we can see which way this vote is going to go," he said.

The council motion not to submit a final bid submission, included an amendment that council would work towards developing it s own cultural programme for the County Tyrone town in 2028.

The motion to not progress with the bid was first put forward last week at a council committee and was deferred until Wednesday's meeting.

At that time, councillors were told following two public engagement sessions in the town in early November, a total of 146 feedback forms were returned to council, six of which were supportive of the bid.

A further 140 forms voiced opposition to Strabane's entry.

articles.title: Four Idaho residents fought a plan to add 100 boat slips at a resort on the Spokane River, then formed an opposition group; the state Supreme Court has dismissed their appeal because the group lacked legal standing
articles.summary: A local campaign to stop a proposed marina expansion on Idaho’s Spokane River has hit an unexpected legal dead end, as the state’s highest court ruled
articles.body: A local campaign to stop a proposed marina expansion on Idaho’s Spokane River has hit an unexpected legal dead end, as the state’s highest court ruled that public opposition alone does not create standing to challenge an administrative decision. Four local residents who originally opposed the development and later formed a nonprofit organization have lost their bid for a judicial review after failing to formally participate as parties in the original permitting process.On November 23, 2026, the Idaho Supreme Court upheld the dismissal of a lawsuit filed by concerned citizens protecting the Spokane River, ruling the organization lacked the legal standing to contest the permit for the marina expansion.Controversy over marina extension planThe case concerns 414 PF Hospitality LLC’s application to the Idaho Department of Lands for an encroachment permit to expand an existing marina at Templin’s Resort, Post Falls. The proposal called for 100 more boat slips and changes to the marina’s infrastructure on the Spokane River.Four residents – Scott and Sheryl Scofield, Jose Jara and Dick Teich – formally objected to the application, raising concerns about its compliance with state law and requesting a public hearing, according to the Idaho Supreme Court’s account.All four attended the December 2024 hearing and spoke out against the development. They later submitted a joint written closing statement under the name Concerned Citizens Against Additional 100 Boat Slips Added to Templin’s Resort on Spokane River. A week later, the residents formed a nonprofit group called Concerned Citizens Protecting the Spokane River, which eventually became the petitioner in their legal fight.No legal footingThe Department of Lands issued the permit and the newly formed organization filed for judicial review of the decision in Kootenai County District Court. The department and 414 PF Hospitality opposed the petition, arguing the nonprofit was not a formal party to the administrative proceedings and thus could not seek judicial review.The district court also agreed that the organization and its members were not aggrieved parties under Idaho’s Lake Protection Act. It then tossed out the petition, denying the nonprofit’s bid for reconsideration.The organization appealed, saying the law gave those who attended public hearings the right to challenge the department's final decisions. It also argued that it could proceed with the case on the basis of associational standing due to the involvement of its four members.Supreme Court clarifies requirements for participationThe Idaho Supreme Court rejected these arguments, noting the difference between members of the public who file objections and those who are formally recognized as parties to administrative proceedings.The Lake Protection Act allows applicants and other aggrieved parties who appear at hearings to seek judicial review. But the court said that just showing up and making public comments does not automatically confer party status.The justices noted that the four residents had not attempted to intervene in the original administrative hearing. They were therefore not parties and had no standing to seek the legal status necessary to challenge the permit.The court also rejected the nonprofit’s claim that it had associational standing because the nonprofit’s members could not establish the requisite standing on their own.Decision on permit upheldThe Idaho Supreme Court upheld the district court’s dismissal in a ruling Nov. 23, allowing the Department of Lands’ approval of the marina expansion to stand.The court awarded appellate costs to the department and 414 PF Hospitality but did not award attorney fees to either party. It also found that the residents had raised legitimate legal arguments in good faith, and were not simply appealing a meritless case.The ruling also further clarifies the procedural standards for challenges to state agency decisions, and makes clear that participation in public hearings does not amount to formal intervention in an administrative case.\Image Courtesy: GoogleYou use AI every day. articles.title: At least 30 killed in Egypt vehicle fire, health ministry says
articles.summary: An additional 15 were injured in blaze after vehicle carrying petroleum products flipped on a major road.
articles.body:
At least 30 people were ⁠⁠killed and ⁠⁠another 25 were injured when a vehicle carrying ‌‌petroleum products overturned and caught fire on a major ring ⁠⁠⁠⁠road in the Egyptian capital, Cairo, the ⁠⁠Health Ministry said on Wednesday.

The fire broke out above a tunnel in the Warraq neighbourhood of Giza’s Imbaba district. The ring road connects key highways across Greater Cairo, linking the governorates of Cairo, ‌‌Giza and Qalyubia.

Local media reported that a truck swerved and hit the central reservation as it overturned, triggering an explosion. The fire has since been extinguished, according to local media.

Egypt’s public prosecutor announced an investigation into the crash and ordered the collection of DNA samples from the victims’ bodies. The judicial office also said 27 vehicles were burned.

The health ministry said 39 ambulances were sent to the site of the incident and that the injured were transferred to nearby hospitals.

The official spokesman for the Egyptian presidency said that President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi “expresses his sincere condolences and sincere sympathy to the families of the victims” and wished them a speedy recovery.

According to an Egyptian Cabinet statement, Prime Minister Mostafa Madbouly offered his condolences to the victims’ families and ordered that their medical expenses be covered by the state.

“The Ministry of Health and Population continues to closely monitor the situation and coordinate with the relevant authorities to ensure that the necessary medical care is provided to the injured,” a ministry statement read.

articles.title: CBS News seeks to settle $20M defamation lawsuit filed by Maryland teenager over Reflecting Pool report
articles.summary: CBS News will enter mediation over a $20 million defamation suit from a Maryland teen who claims the network falsely cast him as a suspected Reflecting Pool vandal.
articles.body: CBS News is attempting to settle a $20 million defamation lawsuit brought by a Maryland teenager who claims he was falsely identified as a person arrested for vandalizing the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool’s lining. The lawsuit, filed in October in U.S. District Court in the District of Columbia, identified the 15-year-old plaintiff simply as "JV." It stated he was not arrested for, or even accused of, vandalizing the memorial, "yet CBS News broadcast and published a story to a national audience that placed JV's image alongside the assertion that five people had been arrested for vandalizing and ‘sabotaging’ the Reflecting Pool, thereby falsely portraying JV as one of the perpetrators of a highly publicized federal crime." The lawsuit stated that CBS "inserted" JV into the controversy in June and "exposed him to extreme embarrassment" and humiliation. JV’s legal team said he has faced "profound" consequences, including embarrassment, humiliation, anxiety, loss of sleep, emotional distress, friends distancing themselves and a continued "fear that CBS's false accusation will follow him through high school and affect his college admissions, athletic opportunities, employment, and future career."
