articles.title: Israeli judges recommend dropping most serious charges against Netanyahu
articles.summary: The Israeli PM says his trial should end after judges said there was little chance of conviction in one of three cases.
articles.body:
Judges in Israel have suggested prosecutors drop bribery charges against Benjamin Netanyahu, potentially handing the caretaker prime minister a boost as he fights for his political survival.

The judges told the attorney general that there was little chance of conviction in the first of three cases he is facing, in which he is accused of granting government favours in exchange for positive media coverage.

They also questioned whether his actions amounted to criminal conduct in a second corruption case, and suggested prosecutors seek a plea deal in a third.

Netanyahu has consistently denied the allegations against him and called on Wednesday for the trial to be ended "immediately".

"Ten years of terrible suffering for me, my family, my son," he said in a televised statement.

"Ten years of incitement to hatred that wounds the soul."

Netanyahu was first charged in 2019, but court proceedings have been prolonged in part by the recent Israel-Gaza war.

The case now under serious doubt, known as Case 4,000, concerns an alleged "reciprocal arrangement" between Netanyahu and the controlling shareholder in Israel's biggest telecoms company. Both denied any wrongdoing.

In a highly unusual step, a judging panel at the Jerusalem District Court summoned Israeli Attorney General Gali Baharav-Miara on Wednesday to express their concerns.

"The chances of conviction are low – to an extent that warrants reconsidering the matter," Judge Rivka Friedman-Feldman told her, Israeli media reported.

The judges also cast doubt on whether Netanyahu's actions, which are subject to a second case – concerning another alleged quid-pro-quo with another media baron, known as Case 2,000 – met the threshold for criminality.

While they left open the possibility of a conviction in the third case: Case 1,000, which alleges Netanyahu acted for the benefit of an Australian billionaire after being gifted cigars and champagne by him.

Netanyahu: What are the corruption charges?

However, the judges told the attorney general that, in the public interest, there needed to be a "rethink" in how the trial should move forward, Israeli media report.

Baharav-Miara said she would consider the judges' recommendations.

It has been six years since Netanyahu became Israel's first sitting prime minister to face a criminal trial.

He has always claimed to be the victim of a political witch-hunt and said on Wednesday that the "fabricated cases" against him were now falling apart.

The cases have continued to progress in court while Netanyahu remained in power throughout the war in Gaza, though judges agreed to reduce the number of hearings due to security concerns around the conflict.

The accusations against him have rocked Israeli politics, fuelling already deep divisions. His trial has coincided with controversial, far-reaching judiciary reforms by Netanyahu's government.

For his opponents, Netanyahu's fear of prison has distorted his decision-making as prime minister and made him especially dependent on his far-right coalition partners to remain in power.

This latest development will give a boost to Netanyahu, whose political opponent Gadi Eisenkot is currently attempting to form a coalition government after an inconclusive general election last month.

While Netanyahu's parliamentary bloc won more seats than that of his rival, both fell short of an outright majority. Israel's president has offered Eisenkot the first chance to form a new administration.

Netanyahu remains subject to an arrest warrant from the International Criminal Court for alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity in Gaza, which he also denies.

articles.title: Netanyahu says corruption trial ‘must end’ as court suggests dropping case
articles.summary: The judges’ recommendations came as Israel’s longest-serving prime minister fights for his political survival.
articles.body:
Israel’s caretaker Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu called for an immediate end to his long-running corruption trial after judges cast doubt on the charges and recommended dropping a case in which he is accused of bribery.

Netanyahu on Wednesday said the “fabricated cases” against him were falling apart, in a televised statement at the Israeli parliament.

The judges’ recommendations came as Israel’s longest-serving prime minister fights for his political survival after inconclusive October 27 elections.

Netanyahu’s main rival, Gadi Eisenkot , has been tasked with forming a government, and if Netanyahu is no longer prime minister, he would lose his leverage to avoid a potential jail sentence.

“Ten years of terrible suffering for me, my family,” Netanyahu said in his speech.

“Ten years of incitement to hatred that wounds the soul. Who will give those years back to us?”

“The trial must end immediately,” he added.

During a hearing in Jerusalem on Wednesday regarding three corruption cases against Netanyahu, judges recommended dropping one, reconsidering another and suggested resolving the third through an agreement, Israeli media reported.

In Case 4000, in which Netanyahu is accused of bribery, fraud and breach of trust, judges indicated there was little chance of a conviction.

That case is considered to be the most serious Netanyahu faces and involves him allegedly offering regulatory favours for a telecoms company in exchange for favourable media coverage.

Netanyahu is alleged to have negotiated with Shaul Elovitch, the controlling shareholder of Israeli telecommunications giant Bezeq, to get positive coverage on his Walla news site in exchange for policies benefitting Bezeq.

On Wednesday, Israeli media reported Judge Rivka Friedman-Feldman saying that proving the bribery charge in that case faced “considerable difficulties”.

Netanyahu, who has been in power on and off for three decades, has repeatedly denied any wrongdoing and denounced the cases as a politically motivated plot against him.

He is the first sitting Israeli prime minister to stand trial.

Israel’s Attorney General Gali Baharav-Miara, who was unusually summoned to the hearing on Wednesday, said she would consider the judges’ recommendations and was ready for either a verdict or a plea deal.

In Case 2000, Netanyahu is accused of fraud and breach of trust over an alleged deal with the owner of Yediot Aharonot for favourable coverage in exchange for curbs on rival newspaper Israel Hayom. Judges on Wednesday questioned whether his actions constituted a crime and recommended reconsidering the case.

In Case 1000, Netanyahu is accused of fraud and breach of trust over allegedly accepting luxury gifts from wealthy individuals in exchange for favours. Judges recommended reaching an agreement to conclude the case.

Netanyahu’s right-wing allies cheered the court’s recommendations and demanded the trial be brought to an end.

“After years of persecution against Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, the time has come to put an end to a trial that was flawed from the outset,” Israel Katz, who is the defence minister in Netanyahu’s caretaker government, wrote on X.

Netanyahu’s corruption trial opened in May 2020.

During his most recent term, which started in late 2022, Netanyahu proposed far-reaching judicial reforms that critics say sought to weaken the courts.

With coalition negotiations under way, Eisenkot’s camp is already trying to start unravelling some of the Netanyahu-era judicial reforms in parliament.

The presidential contender is expected to meet Israeli President Isaac Herzog on Wednesday evening.

His centrist Yashar party said a day earlier that it had agreed to sign a coalition pact with Israel Our Home party after a meeting with its leader Avigdor Lieberman, the first alliance of its kind since the election.

Lieberman has ruled out forming a coalition with Arab-led parties that could hand them a majority in parliament. That has frustrated Democrats chief Yair Golan, who has been pushing Eisenkot to reach a deal with parties representing Israel’s 21 percent Arab minority to make good on his campaign promise to bring down Netanyahu.

Eisenkot also faced a new challenge on Tuesday after the left-wing Democrats suspended coalition talks, further complicating his potential path to power.

The Yashar party leader has until December 6 to form a government under a 28-day mandate, though he could ask for a 14-day extension. If Eisenkot fails, Netanyahu would have an opportunity to do so. If no one is able to form a government, another election will be held next year.

articles.title: Rodeo executive says Americans are hungry for Western culture and the values that come with it
articles.summary: As Western culture surges in popularity, The Hondo Rodeo Fest founder James Trawick says Americans are hungry for family, tradition and experiences that bring people together.
articles.body: At a time when Americans seem to disagree on just about everything, James Trawick thinks there's something that can bring them together: cowboys, country music and a good old-fashioned rodeo. And judging by the success of The Hondo Rodeo Fest, he might be onto something. CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE FROM OUTKICK OUTDOORS "I think across America and the world people are hungry for authentic Western culture," Trawick, co-founder and CEO of The Hondo, told OutKick in an exclusive interview. "Politics has been so all over the place, back and forth, back and forth, and we've been at such odds as a nation — and the world, quite frankly. I think people are just hungry for what we're doing." What they're doing is combining world-class rodeo competition with major country and rock concerts and a celebration of the Western lifestyle. And since launching in Phoenix in 2024, The Hondo has already expanded to New Orleans, with Tampa next on the schedule in February 2027. But for Trawick, the mission goes well beyond putting on a good show. "I think we're all more interested in leaning in toward one another than away from one another," he said. "And it takes something like a Hondo to do that." Americans are hungry for Western culture Of course, Trawick isn't the only one noticing America's renewed fascination with the cowboy lifestyle. From the massive popularity of "Yellowstone" and its spinoffs to the resurgence of traditional country music, Western culture is enjoying a moment in the mainstream spotlight. Artists like Cody Johnson, Zach Top and Lainey Wilson have helped bring cowboy hats, fiddle music and Western traditions back to the forefront of country music. And Trawick believes this particular cultural resurgence has staying power. He pointed to the popularity of the 1980 film "Urban Cowboy," which sparked its own Western fashion craze, but one that was relatively short-lived. "It was hot for a second, but it was kind of a flash in the pan. It only lasted a few years," he said. This time, he believes, something different is happening. "Here we are, whatever this is, six, seven years into when ‘Yellowstone’ hits the scene, and still really bullish on what's going on." Trawick says the demand is reflected in The Hondo's audience. According to ticketing data he cited from Ticketmaster and Experian, approximately 68% of the festival's ticket purchases across its events are family-related. And despite currently operating in only a handful of markets, The Hondo has sold tickets to people from all 50 states and 24 countries. TRACE ADKINS PRAISES PRO FISHING FOR EMBRACING FAITH AND PATRIOTISM: 'THEY'RE NOT AFRAID' "People are flying in internationally to experience this because, one, I think they're just hungry for a wholesome, family-friendly, exciting show," he said. "It's something for the adrenaline junkie, and it's something for parents and grandparents to take their kids and grandkids to." Keeping Western values at the center Of course, when something becomes popular, commercialization usually follows. And with that comes the risk of losing the authenticity that made it appealing in the first place. Trawick is well aware of that danger. "Of course, there's always a risk, and that is so important," he said when asked how The Hondo plans to preserve its Western roots as the business grows. "I've had this conversation with every investor that's come in. At the end of the day, we can get as big as we want to, but if we venture from standing for the anthem, praying before we compete, prioritizing the family — if we get away from those core morals and ethics that come along with Western culture, this community, they won't have it. They won't participate." In other words, he has no intention of abandoning the traditions that define the sport just to make it more palatable to a mainstream audience. In fact, he sees those traditions as part of the appeal. "I wholeheartedly believe that if you say 'yes, ma'am' and 'no, ma'am,' and a man holds a door for a lady, and you just take simple measures of respect, though they may be traditional, I think they're good for us," Trawick said. He continued: "There's respect and dignity in this community like no other community I've ever experienced. This is one that I grew up in, and I just feel like if we can carry a little bit of that out into the world, we can see some healing and some unity." And that's precisely what he hopes to accomplish by bringing Western culture into major American cities. Bringing rodeo to a whole new audience Trawick knows the rodeo world well. He grew up in the sport and competed himself before eventually accepting that a professional career wasn't in the cards. He went on to spend 15 years working in film production, including hunting and fishing projects and content for Western brands. Eventually, he teamed up with business partner, Blake Cody, a former aspiring musician who had since built a trucking business. Together, they came up with an idea to combine their respective worlds into one massive entertainment event. The first Hondo Rodeo Fest drew roughly 60,000 to 65,000 attendees in Phoenix in 2024, according to Trawick. The following year, he said, ticket sales approached 100,000. Part of the appeal is the unusual format. Each day begins with a free street festival featuring Western vendors, food and live music. In the evening, fans head inside for two hours of elite rodeo competition, followed by two major concerts — all included in a single ticket. But the concerts aren't just an added attraction. They're also a way to introduce new fans to the sport. Trawick explained that rodeo is traditionally fragmented across hundreds of sanctioned events, making it difficult for fans to consistently watch the world's best competitors face off. The Hondo instead brings eight of the top contestants in each discipline together to compete for a purse exceeding $1 million. "If you go to the NFL, you go to the NBA, you get to see the best head to head," he explained. "With the Hondo, you got eight of the world's best going head to head. So every single ride, every single run, you're watching somebody that could win that weekend." And he's already seeing evidence that the approach is working. "At our first show, people kind of trickled into the rodeo for the concert. Majority of the reason why they bought the ticket was for the concert," he said. "But when they saw our version of rodeo, they came earlier. You saw it happen across the weekend, just in three days." Trawick also wants the athletes themselves to benefit from that exposure. The Hondo works to help competitors secure media appearances and endorsement opportunities. It even reserves premium concert seating for them, treating the cowboys and cowgirls like the professional sports stars they are. "We carve out part of our floor, our pit, right in front of the stage, just for them," he said. "So it's the most expensive inventory that we have to sell. It's set aside just for them, prioritizing them as the stars that they are." What's next for The Hondo? Following its latest Phoenix event in November, The Hondo is preparing to bring its rodeo-and-music spectacle to Raymond James Stadium in Tampa, Fla., from Feb. 26-28. The lineup includes Cody Johnson, Jason Aldean, Nickelback, Jon Pardi, The Red Clay Strays and Dexter and The Moonrocks. The festival will then return to New Orleans in April and Phoenix in November, with discussions underway about additional markets in 2028 and 2029. But as Trawick looks toward the future, he believes the experience of gathering people together in person is just as important as the entertainment itself. SIGN UP FOR THE DAILY OUTKICK NEWSLETTER "You cannot trade digital for a lived experience in any context," he said. "What you'll feel, what you'll see, the people that you'll meet, all of my words will come to life." And in a country where finding common ground can feel increasingly difficult, Trawick is betting there's still plenty to be found in a rodeo arena. Let's get social. articles.body: A fence erected along a property boundary can become more than a neighbourhood disagreement when it prevents a landowner from accessing part of his own property. In Texas, a dispute that began in 2019 over a fenced-off section of a four-acre tract has resulted in an appeals court upholding an order requiring the encroachments to be removed and a $10,000 statutory damages award.According to a November 12, 2026, memorandum opinion of the Texas Tenth Court of Appeals, available on Justia, the court largely upheld a lower court judgment in favour of Lebedzinski. However, it modified the ruling by removing a declaration that a deed executed by Russell was entirely void and striking $6,450 awarded for attorney’s fees and court costs.How a fence led to a property disputeThe dispute involved neighbouring properties in Walker County, Texas. Lebedzinski owned a four-acre tract, while Russell owned an adjoining 0.5-acre property. According to the lawsuit, Russell erected a fence across the northern end of Lebedzinski’s land and another fence along the western side of a narrow extension, or panhandle, of his property.The fenced-off portion measured approximately 0.4 acres in the original complaint, although the specific section identified in the evidence was a 0.09-acre area. Lebedzinski alleged that the fencing prevented him from accessing and using this part of his property. He attempted to resolve the matter before going to court, sending Russell a demand letter seeking removal of the fence and a partially constructed porch roof that extended onto his land. When those efforts failed, he filed a lawsuit on December 4, 2019, seeking confirmation of his ownership rights and an injunction preventing further interference with his property.The dispute also became more complicated in 2021, when Russell and her husband recorded a warranty deed purporting to transfer three tracts of land to Russell’s mother, Brenda Russell. These included a portion of Lebedzinski’s property and a dirt driveway crossing land belonging to him and another owner.Why the appeals court upheld the removal orderThe trial court ruled in Lebedzinski’s favour after a bench trial on August 28, 2025, which Russell did not attend. It granted an injunction requiring her to remove encroachments from his property and awarded $10,000 in statutory or exemplary damages, along with $6,000 in attorney’s fees and $450 in court costs. Russell challenged the judgment, arguing that she had not received proper notice of the trial, that the evidence did not support the relief granted and that her mother should have been included as a party.The appeals court rejected most of these arguments. It noted that Russell had moved but did not notify the court of her new address until after the trial. She therefore could not rely on the lack of notice to establish a due process violation.On the fencing issue, the court found that testimony and a property survey sufficiently established that the fence occupied part of Lebedzinski’s land and physically prevented him from accessing it. It concluded that monetary compensation alone would not resolve the problem and upheld the permanent injunction requiring removal of the encroachments. The court also rejected Russell’s adverse possession argument, explaining that it was her responsibility to establish the necessary elements of that defence.Why the $10,000 award remainedThe statutory damages award arose not simply from the fence but from the 2021 deed. The appeals court found that Russell had attempted to convey portions of land she did not own, creating a cloud on Lebedzinski’s property title. Under Chapter 12 of the Texas Civil Practice and Remedies Code, a violation involving a fraudulent claim against real property can attract statutory damages of at least $10,000 or the actual damages caused by the violation, whichever is greater. The court explained that this statutory award did not require separate proof of actual financial loss.However, it disagreed with the trial court's decision to declare the entire 2021 deed void. Russell owned the original 0.5-acre tract identified as Tract I, so the deed remained valid as to that property. Her attempted transfer of the other two tracts, which she did not own, had no legal effect but did not invalidate the entire document.The appeals court also removed the $6,000 attorney’s fee award because there was no sufficient evidence establishing that the fees were reasonable and necessary. It struck the $450 court-cost award because an itemised record of those expenses had not been presented. The November 12 decision therefore affirmed the trial court's judgment as modified, preserving the removal order and $10,000 statutory damages award while correcting the deed and fee-related portions of the ruling.You use AI every day.
